Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a foundational approach to training neural networks in reinforcement learning, and it has been applied to contextual bandits and reinforcement learning problems. However, MLE can be unreliable in these settings, as it may prioritize agent actions that lead to poor reward outcomes. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel reward-biased MLE (RBMLE) approach that focuses on the most rewarding data points, thereby enhancing performance. We demonstrate the RBMLE's potential for improving performance in contextual bandits and reinforcement learning by outperforming conventional MLE methods in both discrete and continuous action environments. Additionally, our results show that RBMLE can effectively address the challenges associated with reward misspecification. Overall, the RBMLE offers a practical and efficient solution for training neural agents in real-world settings. interconnected social issues, from individual human behavior to large-scale
socioeconomic systems, evolution of cultural norms, and global social dynamics.

We introduce a novel boundary condition for certain field theories that we call partial soft limits.  Partial soft limits are a type of asymptotic expansion where specific components within the field arrangement remain unchanged while others undergo an asymptotic transformation. Our proposed partial soft limits are inspired by the asymptotic behavior of gluons within the context of soft theorems in QCD, and we demonstrate that they can be applied to various systems including one and three-dimensional scalar fields as well as the Dirac equation for spinor fields. Importantly, we show that the partial soft limit is consistent with the asymptotic expansion of a particular operator, and we provide a mathematical proof that it satisfies an asymptotic expansion property in the context of dimensionless coupling. Our findings suggest that the partial soft limit could be a valuable tool for understanding the asymptotic behavior of field theories with diverse components. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of this boundary condition, including its use in the study of black hole scattering and the asymptotic behavior of massive particles. Finally, we outline some possible research directions for further investigation.

This paper presents a novel approach to visual object detection in documents that leverages deep learning and a custom-trained dataset. The proposed method employs a deep convolutional neural network to locate objects in images, and it is trained on a large dataset of 80,000 bounding boxes with varying object classes. The paper discusses the challenges of using deep convolutional neural networks for document object detection and introduces a new architecture that combines a deep convolutional neural network with a bounding box regression model. The proposed method is evaluated using a large dataset of real-world document images and compared to state-of-the-art techniques for visual object detection. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in detecting visual objects in documents, and it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, the paper highlights the limitations of the current deep convolutional neural network architectures for visual object detection in documents, and it is expected that this work will motivate further research in this area. The proposed method is also expected to improve the accuracy of document image analysis tasks, such as form processing, information extraction, and document understanding. Temporal video modelling is becoming increasingly crucial for handling large-scale videos, and recent advancements have seen a shift towards integrating video modelling with neural network architectures. These efforts have led to the development of various models, such as the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) family, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN), and the Long Term-Dependent Convolutional (LTC) network. Despite their success, these models have significant limitations, including the slow convergence of LSTMs and the high computational cost of TCNs and LTC. In this paper, we introduce a novel model called Gradient Forward Network (GF-Net) that can efficiently handle large-scale temporal data. Our model is based on a new forward network architecture that can learn temporal patterns and capture long-term dependencies with high accuracy and low computational cost. By using a combination of fully connected layers and a new forward network architecture, GF-Net can learn both local and global temporal patterns, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in a range of applications such as video classification, object detection, and action recognition. Our experiments show that GF-Net outperforms existing models, achieving accuracy gains of up to 2.5% and reducing computational time by up to 60%. The proposed model is also robust to hyperparameter tuning and can be easily adapted to handle large-scale videos, making it a promising solution for temporal video modelling. In addition, we release the code of our model to facilitate future research in this area. Our work is expected to open up new avenues for developing efficient large-scale temporal video models. We propose the "discrete adaptive rejection technique" (DART), a new algorithm for identifying a specific subset of items from a larger pool of items that satisfy a specific criterion. The proposed solution is particularly relevant to large data sets such as online search engine results, where only the top K items match the search query. DART is designed to efficiently process these results, focusing on the top K relevant items while rejecting the less relevant ones. To achieve this goal, DART is formulated as a sequential decision-making process where each step aims to identify whether the current item is part of the top K relevant results. The algorithm leverages a dynamic programming approach to minimize computational overhead. We demonstrate that DART is a more efficient solution than traditional methods, such as the top K operator in SQL, which evaluates all items. We also show that DART is a more accurate solution than heuristics, such as the "first word" heuristic. Researchers have proposed several distribution alignment methods to mitigate the issue of imperfect reward estimates in imitation learning. Although these methods are effective, they can still lead to misaligned policies, resulting in slow learning. Building on prior work, we introduce a new approach called SoftDICE, a two-stage method that uses a soft update to align the distribution of expert and student behavior. SoftDICE involves an initial, offline phase where the student learns from the expert without interacting with the environment, followed by a online, interactive stage where the student learns from an expert policy generated through the offline stage. Through theoretical analysis and experimental testing, we demonstrate that SoftDICE can align the distribution more effectively than existing methods, leading to improved policy transfer and faster convergence on a range of tasks. Moreover, SoftDICE can be easily integrated into other distribution alignment methods, making it a valuable addition to the field. In experiments, we show that SoftDICE can outperform state-of-the-art methods on several challenging tasks, including robotic manipulation and reinforcement learning benchmarks. Additionally, SoftDICE can be combined with other alignment methods to achieve superior results. The code for SoftDICE is available for public access.

The Supremacy Calculus is a proof system that extends the capabilities of the NP-complete NP-unification, allowing for the derivation of more complex unification algorithms. It serves as a theoretical framework for developing optimal sequent calculi for various unification theories. Notably, its applicability goes beyond unification, as it can be used to study other mathematical structures, including lattices and quasi-ordered sets. This paper focuses on two key aspects of the Supremacy Calculus: simplifying proofs and eliminating redundant steps. Specifically, it introduces a new technique to streamline AC simplifications in proofs and identifies closure redundancy, a redundancy that can be automatically eliminate using a straightforward method. Moreover, it is shown that eliminating closure redundancy has the same effect as restricting the number of AC inductive steps to a single step per variable. This, in turn, enables the derivation of more efficient sequent calculus for solving the word problem in various algebraic structures. This paper also explores the connection between closure redundancy and other redundancy elimination techniques, such as subformula property redundancy. It is hoped that this work will facilitate further research into the Supremacy Calculus and its applications to other mathematical structures. This paper explores the possibilities of implementing optimizations for quantum interpreters, which are the base infrastructure for all quantum programming. As the use of quantum programs becomes more widespread, it is essential to improve the performance of these interpreters to make high-performance quantum computing accessible to a broader audience. The researchers discuss various techniques that can be employed to achieve this goal and also propose a set of benchmarks to measure the effectiveness of these optimizations.

The authors discuss the following optimization strategies:

  1.  Instruction fusion: This optimization technique combines multiple instructions into a single more efficient instruction, which can be applied to quantum programs. The researchers demonstrate the feasibility of this approach by fusing adjacent Hadamard gates and demonstrating the impact on various quantum algorithms.
  2.  Reordering of quantum operations: This optimization strategy involves rearranging the order of quantum operations to achieve better performance. The researchers illustrate this by optimizing the order of operations in the Grover's algorithm and demonstrating significant speedup.
  3.  Elimination of redundant operations: This optimization technique identifies and eliminates unnecessary quantum operations to achieve faster execution times. The researchers demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by eliminating redundant gates in the quantum Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm.
  4.  Instruction expansion: This optimization strategy involves breaking down more complex quantum instructions into simpler instructions, which can actually result in a performance boost. The researchers illustrate this by breaking down the Fredkin gate into three simpler gates, leading to a significant increase in quantum algorithm execution speed.
  5.  Quantum interpreter self-modification: This optimization technique allows the quantum interpreter to modify its own behavior to achieve better performance. The researchers propose a mechanism to achieve this, but caution that its effectiveness is highly dependent on the specific quantum algorithm being executed.
  6.  Compilation of quantum programs: This optimization strategy involves converting quantum programs into more efficient machine code that can be executed by the quantum interpreter. The researchers propose a compiler back-end for Qiskit to achieve this goal. The researchers also emphasize the need for a rigorous evaluation of the effectiveness of these optimizations in real-world quantum algorithms to ensure their practical utility. The growing field of algorithmic misinformation detection has significant social implications, yet its development lacks sufficient consideration of its effects on marginalized groups. Consequently, researchers and developers are failing to adequately address the potential negative consequences of their systems. To address this oversight, we analyzed the current state of algorithmic misinformation detection, examining how it intersects with social justice, particularly for marginalized communities. Through an in-depth analysis of algorithms, stakeholders, and potential harms, we identified key areas of concern and proposed a framework to guide the design of fairer and more equitable misinformation detection systems. Our findings suggest that such systems can cause harm, often in ways that is not being acknowledged by the algorithmic misinformation detection community. We propose that our framework can serve as a starting point for addressing the social justice implications of these systems, guiding the creation of more equitable technology. Ultimately, we hope that this work will inspire further discussion and action within the algorithmic misinformation detection community to create more just outcomes.

GANs have become increasingly popular for generating synthetic data in various domains. Despite their benefits, GAN training can be challenging due to the inherent instability caused by a problem known as mode collapse. This issue arises when the model converges to a limited set of patterns instead of the desired distribution. Several methods have been proposed to overcome mode collapse, but they often lack a rigorous theoretical framework, and their effectiveness is not consistently demonstrated. This paper presents a theoretical analysis of mode collapse based on Hessian eigenvalues, providing a deeper understanding of GAN training instability. Our empirical study reveals that mode collapse is more likely to occur when the Hessian matrix has a lower condition number, and we evaluate the condition number of different architectures and training techniques to identify effective strategies for preventing mode collapse. Through this research, we aim to provide a solid foundation for developing robust mode-collapse prevention techniques. Our findings are expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of GAN training instability and the development of more reliable methods to prevent it. In real-world networks, the connections between different layers often hold vital information about the entities within those layers. This is particularly evident in various fields, such as understanding the spread of diseases or identifying relationships between individuals in social networks. This means that analyzing the links between different layers in a multiplex network can reveal valuable insights about the entities within that network. This paper introduces a novel approach to this analysis, an unsupervised learning method that utilizes a multiplex embedding model to identify patterns of correlation and contrast between different layers in a network. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in a multiplex network of European cities connected through trade relationships, as well as a multiplex network of actors representing countries, connected through co-authorship relationships, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in our experiments. Our findings also shed new light on the relationships between European cities and their co-authoring actors. This is achieved through a comprehensive evaluation of our method's performance on both artificial and real-world datasets. Our results show that the links identified by our method are more accurate and consistent than those produced by existing methods. Our approach is also scalable and can be applied to large networks with many layers, as demonstrated by our experiments on a network of 200 European cities with 3 layers. This note demonstrates that polar codes have an inherent property of being the most efficient codes for use with the polar decoding method, and existing work has only provided upper bounds for their error rates. To fill this gap, we have developed a new method to calculate the error rates of polar codes under the polar decoding system, and in doing so, we have found that these rates actually reach their lowest minimum when polar codes are used. Furthermore, we have also established that any significant improvement in the effectiveness of other decoding systems would automatically result in a comparable improvement in the effectiveness of polar codes. As a result of this discovery, we conclude that polar codes remain the most efficient codes for use with the polar decoding system, and in fact, remain the most efficient codes for use with any decoding system. To further validate our findings, we have also established a lower bound for the error rates of symmetric codes and have determined that a specific type of code, known as a symmetric polar code, achieves the lowest minimum error rate of all symmetric codes. By defining a generic Hamiltonian framework and adapting the Schrödinger equation to pseudotime, we derive the geometric unitary approach and establish its connection to real-time quantum mechanics via the geometric mapping function. Moreover, we examine the feasibility of pseudotime-based experiments and discuss the implications of pseudotime for our understanding of time. Finally, we speculate on the possibility that pseudotime could be a fundamental aspect of nature. This study introduces a novel fusion method for extracting detailed information
from low-resolution images combined with high-resolution spectral data in the
hyperspectral domain. The proposed approach, a deep gradient optimization
network, seamlessly integrates the entire fusion process into a single,
differentiable module. The deep gradient optimization network comprises two
key components: a pan-sharpening module and a denoising module. The former
optimizes high-resolution pan images by leveraging the gradients of denoised
hyperspectral images, while the latter refines the high-resolution image through
iterative denoising processes, combining both color and spatial details.

network in achieving superior outcomes compared to existing pan-sharpening
techniques. The proposed approach is also adaptable to a variety of applications,

We introduce a novel algorithm, ISLET, for estimating low-rank tensors from noisily observed samples. Unlike conventional methods, ISLET efficiently addresses high-dimensional tensors with a large number of variables, boasting polynomial time complexity and optimal sample requirements. This is achieved through a novel importance sketching technique that significantly reduces the computational cost of tensor estimation. We show that ISLET outperforms existing tensor estimation approaches, both statistically and computationally, and its performance is further enhanced when combined with other methods. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of ISLET in comparison to the current state-of-the-art tensor estimation techniques. The proposed approach is also generalized to various related tensor tasks, such as sparse tensor estimation, tensor regression, and tensor independence testing. The proposed algorithms and codes are available at https://github.com/boomasanjanin/ISLET. Further theoretical and practical analyses of the methods are provided in the supplementary materials. The authors also offer a perspective on the future directions of tensor estimation research. Deep neural networks have been widely adopted for place recognition in autonomous driving, leveraging LiDAR scans due to their ability to function in adverse weather conditions. Nevertheless, the traditional 2D CNN approach has limitations when utilizing 3D LiDAR data, as it fails to capture global spatial information. To address this, we introduce AttDLNet, an innovative network that combines attention and graph neural networks for reliable place recognition. By employing a graph neural network to model point clouds and an attention-based network to monitor the learning process, AttDLNet effectively captures global spatial information. Our model's efficacy is demonstrated through extensive experiments on multiple datasets under varying conditions. The mechanical characteristics of soft materials are typically described by non-linear constitutive models. However, there is no universally accepted model, and the choice of one over others is often based on convenience rather than a thorough evaluation. This paper presents a method for selecting the most suitable constitutive model by applying Bayesian inference to experimental data. The approach involves calculating the posterior probability of each model based on maximum likelihood estimates and then using this information to determine the optimal model along with its key parameters. The method has been tested using both simulated data and real-world measurements from biaxial tests on porcine aortic valves. The results show that the optimal model can be accurately identified, even when the data is contaminated with significant noise. The method has potential for use in evaluating a range of constitutive models and could facilitate a more informed approach to selecting the optimal model for specific applications. (Careful on the Internet), which aimed to educate the public about the risks of social 
manipulation and online misinformation. The report outlines the methodology, 
demographics of the respondents, and findings of the survey, highlighting the 
effectiveness of the campaign in reaching the target audience and having a positive effect 
on increasing awareness among citizens about the existence, nature, and prevention of social 
manipulation. Furthermore, the report presents the survey's questions, along with the response options, 
allowing for easy reference and comparison with other surveys addressing similar topics.

We analyzed the chemical composition of the gas surrounding the protoplanetary disk of the star TW Hya, which contains a large planet likely influencing its evolution. Using ALMA data, we calculated the abundance ratios of carbon, oxygen, and carbon-to-nitrogen within the disk, finding that these elements are enriched by a factor of 3 to 4 above solar levels. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is significantly enriched, being two to three times greater than the protosolar value. These findings are consistent with the predictions of planet formation models, which suggest that the disk's composition is altered by a massive planet. The observed enrichment of carbon and nitrogen is attributed to the sub-stellar mass of the planet and the presence of a dead zone in the disk, which allows volatile elements to be accreted onto the planet. Consequently, this leads to the accumulation of carbon and nitrogen in the planet. To effectively learn programming, students must be able to seamlessly transition between reading, visualizing, and coding, which involves executing mental images in a sequence of events. However, little research has explored the cognitive process of linking these concepts together. To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted a neuroimaging study with 31 participants to investigate the brain's brain regions associated with cognitive integration. By using a dual-task paradigm, we measured brain activity while participants read, visualized, and coded on either real or imagined text, which revealed significant findings. Our results indicate that when a subject is coding or visualizing, there is greater activity in regions such as the left occipital lobe, and the left inferior frontal and posterior parietal regions, which are involved in language and spatial processing. Conversely, when a subject is reading, visualizing, or coding, there is greater activity in areas involved in working memory, such as the prefrontal and lateral occipital regions. Our study's findings provide valuable insights into the cognitive process of learning programming, which can inform the development of a neurotechnological framework to aid in education. Ultimately, this research aims to enhance our understanding of how neurotechnologies can be used to support human learning and development. This paper provides an overview of speedrunning and presents a framework for developing AI-based navigation systems that can learn and replicate human navigation strategies. 

Additionally, the paper discusses the obstacles that need to be overcome in order to develop an effective AI system that can learn and perform speedruns in various video games. Finally, the paper outlines a set of challenges that can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of AI-based navigation systems. These challenges require a high level of precision and are difficult to complete with current human capabilities.

We introduce SART, a comprehensive dataset with extensive word relationships 
encompassing Tatar, English, Russian, and Uzbek languages. The SART dataset 
includes 1.7 million Tatar sentences, each paired with an English equivalent, 
containing 1,017,000 unique Tatar words. The SART dataset features five key 
evaluation tasks: semantic similarity, analogies, detecting word relationships, 
extracting word sets, and determining word frequency. These tasks enable thorough 
analysis of Tatar word embeddings, ultimately benefiting the development of 
word embeddings tailored to the Tatar language and contributing to the growth 
of word embeddings suitable for languages similar to Tatar. SART is now freely 
accessible at https://github.com/arslancan/sart. A baseline evaluation using 
common word embeddings demonstrates the potential of SART in assessing word 
embeddings' performance. The accompanying report documents the creation of

introduced dataset, and provides detailed statistics about the resource. The 
dataset is accompanied by a Python API for seamless usage. The SART dataset

Recent advancements in deep learning have seen a significant surge in transformer-based models, particularly in medical image segmentation tasks. Despite these breakthroughs, these models often struggle with the "data scarcity" problem when working with limited medical image datasets. By leveraging these attention mechanisms, DAE-Former enhances segmentation performance by identifying key features and spatially normalizing them across input images. Experimental results demonstrate that DAE-Former outperforms existing models in medical image segmentation tasks, achieving notable improvements on standard datasets. Our findings are supported by visual analysis, which highlights the benefits of our proposed dual attention approach. Overall, DAE-Former offers a compelling solution for healthcare professionals seeking to improve the accuracy of medical image segmentation tasks with limited, high-quality datasets available. We investigate the super-resolution problem of recovering a discrete set of point sources from noisy, one-dimensional measurements obtained via Fourier sampling. We introduce a novel, computationally efficient algorithm for solving this issue without requiring any prior knowledge of the underlying data and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical simulations. The performance of this algorithm is evaluated using synthetic data and compared against existing state-of-the-art methods, revealing its effectiveness in challenging scenarios where traditional approaches struggle. Additionally, the algorithm's ability to solve related inverse problems is also considered and developed. We provide theoretical support for the algorithm through the derivation of a convergence rate, obtained via an application of the restricted isoperimetric inequality. The convergence analysis relies on a geometric representation of the algorithm's iterations, treating the updated estimates as the peaks of an evolving surface under the influence of a gradient flow. By analyzing the time-evolution of the surface's peaks, we establish a restricted isoperimetric inequality for the algorithm's iterations, which in turn enables us to derive a convergence rate. OG-SPACE is designed to efficiently simulate large cancer evolution models on parallel computing systems, significantly reducing the time required for simulation. OG-SPACE achieves this efficiency by employing a variety of optimizations, including the use of spatial data structures, parallelizing stochastic processes, and reducing unnecessary computations. OG-SPACE has been successfully applied to a complex cancer evolution model, producing accurate results in a fraction of the time required by other methods, thus paving the way for its use in a wide range of applications. This configuration leads to nodes in its self-consistently determined energy spectrum at the Fermi level, thus classifying it as a node-line superconductor. To validate these conclusions, experiments were performed, including angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which revealed a Fermi surface consistent with theoretical predictions. Additionally, resistivity and specific heat measurements revealed superconducting temperatures of approximately 0.76 K and 0.84 K, respectively. These findings are supported by density functional theory calculations, which predict a superconducting critical temperature of 0.77 K. Moreover, it shows that node-line nodal superconductors can be realized in 2D systems. Our research also highlights the importance of considering the electronic structure's anisotropy in layered materials for understanding their electronic properties. Finally, it suggests that CaSb$_2$ is a prime candidate for studying unconventional superconductivity resulting from orbital-selective superconductivity. Such research could lead to a deeper understanding of superconductivity's microscopic mechanisms. This approach has been successfully applied to predict and validate the electronic structure of CaSb$_2$ using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Our research thus opens up new avenues for understanding the electronic structure of layered materials and discovering unconventional superconductors. This study has significant implications for understanding the electronic structure of other materials with similar properties. Our results suggest that other materials like LaP and CeP, with similar Fermi surface configurations, could also be explored as potential node-line superconductors. Furthermore, it demonstrates improved performance over a conventional stochastic gradient descent approach in recognizing patterns in binary images. The underlying neural update equations are also derived using a moment closure approximation. We've developed a novel network trimming approach based on resource redistribution, which optimizes network efficiency. By prioritizing the preservation of the most critical routes through a maximum flow calculation, we transfer the remaining resources to a secondary pool, from which we can assign them to the remaining paths in a flexible manner, achieving optimal utilization of available resources. This method provides a reliable means of maintaining the integrity of specific network paths, even in scenarios where the infrastructure is severely degraded. Additionally, we've adapted this approach to accommodate a variety of network path objective functions, including the most direct routes, the shortest routes, and routes that minimize cost, all while ensuring the reliability of the network. Through numerical analysis, we've demonstrated that our method yields optimal results and outperforms existing network trimming techniques in terms of efficiency. The proposed algorithm has been successfully implemented in a widely used network analysis software, further expanding its capabilities. Federated learning, an emerging machine learning technique, enables multiple entities to collaborate on training a model without exchanging sensitive data.  Federated learning, however, often requires each entity to have sufficient data to train a model effectively.  To address this limitation, researchers have proposed customized federated learning, a technique that allows a central model to be tailored to the unique needs of each entity.  To further advance this approach, we introduce a novel method using hypernetworks to generate customized models for each entity.  Experimental results demonstrate that hypernetworks-based federated learning can lead to improved model accuracy and convergence rates compared to traditional methods.  Furthermore, our findings suggest that hypernetworks can effectively handle imbalanced data distributions by adapting to varying degrees of model customization.  Ultimately, our research highlights the potential of hypernetworks to offer a more efficient and adaptable framework for customized federated learning, particularly in scenarios with limited local data. The increasing use of surveillance cameras in public spaces has made head detection a crucial aspect of intelligent video analysis. However, existing methods often struggle with accuracy and robustness in real-world scenarios. This paper presents the motion-aware pseudo siamese network (MPSN), a novel approach that integrates motion features for improved head detection. MPSN consists of a motion estimation block, a motion feature extraction block, and a head identification block. The motion estimation block generates optical flow maps, which are leveraged by the motion feature extraction block to extract dynamic features. These dynamic features are then combined with static features to enhance the representation learning capability of the head identification block. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the MPSN's state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets and its superiority in handling diverse head sizes and occlusions. The introduction of hardware-based security features has significantly contributed to safeguarding applications against malicious code. However, the lack of a unified testing framework hampers the evaluation of these security features across different processor architectures. To address this limitation, we present a comprehensive test suite for ensuring memory safety, adaptable to various platforms and capable of identifying vulnerabilities in memory access. This test suite comprises 55 distinct test cases, each simulating a range of memory-related scenarios, including incorrect dereferences and improper memory interactions. To validate its effectiveness, we applied our test suite to three prominent processor architectures: Intel Core i7, AMD Ryzen 5, and ARM Cortex-A53. The results demonstrated that the test suite can successfully identify and reproduce vulnerabilities in these architectures, thereby facilitating the assessment of memory safety on diverse processor designs. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and constraints associated with replicating our findings across different processor architectures. To promote the advancement of secure processor research, we make our test suite publicly available in a GitHub repository. As the adoption of hardware-based security features becomes more widespread, a standardized testing framework is essential to ensure the reliability of these security features across various processor architectures. By sharing our test suite, we aim to contribute to the development of efficient evaluation methods for assessing the security features of modern processors. Similarly, we encourage the research community to develop and utilize testing frameworks that can accurately identify vulnerabilities in memory access. By doing so, we can ensure the reliability of security features and safeguard sensitive data from malicious threats. This study introduces a probability model for censored data and assesses the effectiveness of the Kolmogorov, Anderson-Darling, and Li, Lin, and Shen goodness-of-fit tests to evaluate the model's performance. Building on the principle of maximum likelihood estimation, the model's parameters are determined through the maximum likelihood approach when data is complete, and through the method of conditional maximum likelihood for censored data. The model's reliability is then evaluated using the mentioned goodness-of-fit tests, and through the comparison of estimated model parameters with their actual values, known as the "bull's eye" method. The results of the model's performance are demonstrated using data from a hypothetical manufacturing process, and supported by graphical analysis. Further, the effectiveness of the proposed model is compared to the Weibull distribution in an attempt to determine which distribution better describes the data. The comparison reveals that the empirical probability model outperforms the Weibull distribution in most cases. Finally, the study provides practical guidelines for applying the proposed model in real-world reliability analysis. The companion R package 'empprob' facilitates the implementation of the model, allowing users to access its key functions, including empirical probability plotting, goodness-of-fit tests, and the bull's eye method. In this research, we investigate the capabilities of cutting-edge image restoration models in handling complex, moving scenes. To achieve this goal, we introduce a new dataset called Dynamic Image Restoration (DIR), which consists of challenging video sequences containing various types of motion. By evaluating existing image restoration models on DIR, we identify significant knowledge gaps in current research. To address these gaps, we develop a novel approach that can effectively handle multiple types of motion within a single image. Our solution, termed Joint Motion and Restoration (JMRE), is a deep learning-based framework that can simultaneously detect and correct motion, as well as restore image quality. JMRE achieves state-of-the-art results on DIR and outperforms existing models on other standard datasets as well. Notably, JMRE also demonstrates superior performance in terms of generalizability when compared to previous research. Our contributions will be demonstrated through the improved performance of DIR-trained models on various datasets, as well as the enhanced generalizability of our models on datasets such as KITTI. We introduce an optimization-based approach to the reduction method of the AMG algorithm, incorporating a coarse solver benefit estimation similar to the RAGE method and a policy learning through reinforcement learning. This policy is expressed as a differentiable algorithm, where each decision is a differentiable function of the solver benefits. We optimize the policy using a gradient descent method on the expected benefit of the solver. We also propose an approach to reduce the computational overhead of the policy by using a hierarchical tree of subspaces and only updating the upper levels. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on various problems and compare it to other reduction methods and RL algorithms for AMG coarsening. Our results show that the policy outperforms other RL algorithms and some reduction methods, particularly on large problems. We also observe that the hierarchical subspace approach reduces the computational overhead of the policy while maintaining its effectiveness. Furthermore, our approach is flexible and can be applied to various other reduction methods, such as the hybrid method and the nested dissection approach. In the context of Bayesian optimal transfer learning, we investigate the issue of estimating generalization errors in settings where only a limited number of target environment samples are available. English-French translation tasks. Our experiments show that this approach leads

The MASCARA-1 star, a late-A type, hosts a hot Jupiter gas giant, detected through the high-precision TESS photometric survey. Subsequent research utilizing Spitzer space telescope thermal imaging revealed a possible 1.5-day period modulation in the star's flux, attributed to the planet's orbital pattern around the star near its polar axis. This near-polar orbit is further supported by CHEOPS transit observations, yielding a precise orbital period of 1.0516 days. The CHEOPS data analysis also revealed a significant secondary eclipse time shift, suggesting the planet's near-polar orbit and, potentially, the star's internal dynamics. The latter possibility implies that MASCARA-1 may be a binary system, warranting further investigation. The CHEOPS data also enabled the derivation of the planet's radius and orbital distance, enabling the calculation of its surface gravity and heat flux, and ultimately yielding an age of approximately 1.1 billion years for the system. This near-polar orbit is a rare phenomenon, with only a few other known instances, and its occurrence in this system is further highlighted by the presence of a possible dayside rebound effect in the planet's atmosphere. The MASCARA-1 system serves as a prime target for future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope, offering opportunities to study planetary atmospheres and evolutionary processes in detail. Reinforcement learning algorithms have been successfully applied to a wide range of tasks, but they often falter in situations where the reward signal is delayed or rare. To address this limitation, we introduce the Temporal Transition Reinforcement Learning framework, which integrates reinforcement learning with supervised learning of temporal dynamics. By combining these approaches, we enable agents to learn not only what actions to take, but also when to take them, by modeling the evolution of states over time. This approach is particularly effective in tasks where the immediate state changes provide valuable clues about the optimal action, such as when rare rewards are scattered across a vast and varied environment. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms both traditional reinforcement learning and temporal dynamics alone in these challenging and diverse tasks. This breakthrough has significant implications for improving performance in real-world applications, where the reward signal is often late to arrive. The development of text generation models that insert specific object categories, such as animals, has been a significant area of research. This research focuses on entity-guided text generation, which involves embedding entities and their corresponding categories into generated text. This is achieved by incorporating cross-attention between entities and the generated text. However, existing models have limitations in two areas: (1) entities and categories are manually selected during training, and (2) the cross-attention mechanism can only focus on one entity at a time. This research proposes a novel approach called EC-Transducer, which addresses these issues. EC-Transducer introduces an encoder-decoder model that can automatically select relevant entities and categories, and incorporate them into the generated text. The model uses a transformer-based encoder to represent entities and categories, and a transformer-based decoder to generate text. The model also employs a multi-head attention mechanism that can focus on all entities and categories simultaneously. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of EC-Transducer, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in terms of BLEU scores. The model also shows promising results in generating coherent text that accurately reflects the entities and categories. This research is significant as it addresses the limitations of previous models and provides a more efficient and effective approach to entity-guided text generation. In a competitive digital advertising landscape, the task of creating optimal auction price designs for high-frequency sponsored search becomes increasingly complex.
To address this challenge, this research develops a novel approach to designing auction price mechanisms for real-time electronic markets with frequent price changes.
By leveraging a Markov decision process, the design can be broken down into distinct sub-problems that are efficiently solved using standard methods.
The outcome is a dynamic pricing mechanism that adapts to real-time market conditions, and experimental analysis confirms its ability to achieve higher revenue than established fixed price designs used by platforms like Lazada. Moreover, the design exhibits robustness to errors in the underlying transition model. The proposed framework has been implemented in real-time on Lazada's sponsored search platform, resulting in notable revenue increases of up to 2.37% over a 3-month period spanning 2020. A key concept in computing, the future result or promise, is formally defined as an event that has not yet occurred but is certain to happen. However, the nature of this concept differs across various computational models. This paper examines the concept of promises in different computational models, demonstrates that it is well-defined in well-known models such as sequential, linearizable, and causally-bracketing systems, but may not be in weak memory models like SC memory and release consistency models. It then uses a graph theory model to show that an SC memory system can be considered as a set of independent, predictable events, and that this understanding can be applied to other related models. Furthermore, the research shows that events in these models can be considered reliable and that their causal relationships are predictable, and it also establishes a connection between these models and an event sequence theory, allowing for a more in-depth analysis of the events and their consequences. Additionally, the research provides a set of tools for analyzing the events and their relationships in different computational models. We investigate non-log-concave sampling distributions by formulating a novel
variational approach that relates to the Hessian of the associated target density.
This new perspective allows for a precise analysis of the convergence of Langevin
Monte Carlo in first-order. Specifically, we establish a convergence rate to the
stationary distribution using a Lyapunov function tailored to the target, which can
be constructed from the Hessian's behavior and function majorization schemes. 
Furthermore, we develop an efficient method for calculating the Lyapunov function 
in practice, particularly for cases involving simple rational functions as targets. 
The findings are validated through numerical experiments on a range of non-log-concave
distributions. In cases where the Hessian information is unavailable, we suggest an
alternative method for Lyapunov function computation based on a specific class of 
distributions known as generalized P\'olya distributions. This work is the first
to provide a rigorous first-order convergence guarantee for Langevin Monte Carlo in
non-log-concave settings. The novel variational approach also offers a broader 
framework for analyzing the convergence of Langevin dynamics in general scenarios. 
Additionally, the Lyapunov function developed here can be utilized to establish 
convergence bounds for other sampling algorithms, such as the Langevin version of 
the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm. The corresponding code can be accessed 
at https://github.com/sarveshwaradha/lyapunov-certification-langevin. 
This work is complemented by a companion paper (arXiv:2101.10819) that presents 
numerical results in higher dimensions. 
The authors also provide an extension of this work to the Gibbs sampler in a companion 
paper (arXiv:2107.04453). Finally, we establish a convergence result for Langevin dynamics 
in the context of Poincar\'e inequalities in a companion paper (arXiv:2107.04462).

This paper introduces a distributed reinforcement learning approach, referred to as multi-stream reinforcement learning (MSRL), which leverages data fragments from multiple sources to create a unified learning environment. MSRL addresses the challenge of learning from distributed data streams with varying lengths and rates, potentially containing time-related or sequential data. MSRL employs a two-stage data fusion strategy, initially merging data fragments based on time or content, followed by a second stage that aggregates learning outcomes from the fused data. MSRL was tested using three synthetic environments, and its performance was compared with that of traditional distributed reinforcement learning methods. MSRL was found to deliver improved results in terms of sample efficiency and learning speed, particularly when dealing with unevenly distributed rewards. Furthermore, MSRL was found to be resilient to data stream disruptions, including delayed or missing observations, and its ability to learn from variable data rates, potentially significantly higher than traditional methods, was also demonstrated. The effectiveness of MSRL was further validated by its application to real-world robotic navigation tasks. This highlights the potential of MSRL to deliver robust and efficient learning outcomes in complex, dynamic environments. The proposed approach, MSRL, provides a novel and efficient distributed reinforcement learning solution for applications involving diverse data streams and environments with variable dynamics. As the use of autonomous systems becomes more widespread, ensuring their safety is an increasingly critical issue. One approach to enhancing safety is the incorporation of safety supervisors that monitor and intervene in critical system functions. Research has developed multiple such supervisors, but they often rely on unrealistic assumptions about the systems and environments they interact with. This limitation makes it difficult to assess their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. This paper presents the FindSafe framework, a comprehensive testing tool for safety supervisors, and demonstrates its application in evaluating the performance of three commonly used supervisors in complex simulation environments that mimic real-world challenges. The results show that these supervisors can fail to guarantee safe system behavior in such scenarios, highlighting the importance of rigorous testing in assessing their effectiveness. This study aims to facilitate the development of robust and reliable safety supervisors by guiding future research and highlighting the need for rigorous evaluation. The framework and associated testing setup are intended to aid in the comprehensive assessment of safety supervisors. Our findings also show that TNT's capabilities are not limited to identifying TNT's tunneled IP addresses; it can detect any IP address, including those associated with various routing systems. Our experiments, conducted on real networks, including within and across organizations, have validated TNT's capabilities. Our code and the results of our experiments are available for public access. The developed approach can be seamlessly integrated into high-resolution imaging techniques to generate detailed three-dimensional models of porous media. requiring significant time and memory resources. In contrast, traditional video 
compression methods offer a more efficient alternative. In this research, 
a novel hybrid system, Gemino, is presented that combines the benefits of both 
neural and traditional video compression techniques. By integrating the robust 
features of neural models with the efficiency of modern codecs, Gemino aims to 
outperform state-of-the-art solutions in video conferencing applications. 
This hybrid approach is evaluated through comprehensive tests, including 
subjective and objective assessments, which confirm that Gemino excels in video 
quality while maintaining comparable encoding and decoding times.

baseline and a 10% improvement in objective quality, all while meeting the 
requirements for real-time video conferencing. Our findings are expected to 
encourage further research in neural compression and foster its practical 
implementation in future communication systems. The proposed Gemino model will 
be made available to the research community upon publication. This paper is

The Indo-Aryan family's diverse member, Bhojpuri, comprises several languages including Magahi, Maithili, and Bhojpuri proper, along with their dialects. As the languages spoken predominantly in northern India and southern Nepal, they hold significant cultural importance among the local population. Despite their relevance, however, limited research has been conducted on these languages due to a shortage of available resources. To bridge this gap, this study compiles a comprehensive set of resources for Bhojpuri, Magahi, and Maithili, which includes over 1,200,000 tokens in written form, 1,200,000 tokens in spoken dialects, and 1,500,000 tokens in spoken Magahi dialects. The study also presents various statistical and linguistic analysis results, and baseline performance on three distinct tasks: automatic language identification, language modeling, and machine translation. The collected resources are expected to serve as a valuable asset for future research and contribute to a more diverse linguistic landscape. This paper proposes a preliminary open standard for regulating social robots, 
addressing ethical concerns in a manner that prioritizes user sovereignty and 
transparent governance. The proposed standard incorporates a 'black box' that 
promotes transparency while safeguarding users' personal data and aims to establish 
a regulatory framework that is open, equitable, and human-centered, giving 
particular emphasis to protecting human dignity. The proposed standard is designed 
to empower users and promote social Robot Regulation that is inclusive, humane, 
and grounded in the principles of respect for human dignity. The proposed open 
standard is intended to be an evolving draft, thus encouraging critical comments 
and contributions from relevant stakeholders. Ultimately, our goal is to create a 
regulatory framework that is open, dynamic, and human-centric, enabling robots 
to interact with humans in a manner that is respectful and humane. 

This paper is part of a larger research project examining the ethics of social 
robots, particularly in relation to the potential risks and benefits of such 
systems. The proposed open standard is a key component of this project, aiming to 
contribute to a more inclusive and humane regulatory environment for social robots. 

We welcome any comments, contributions, or criticisms from relevant stakeholders, 
as this proposed open standard is subject to revision and improvement based on 
feedback from the community.

Seismic interpretation is an arduous task that heavily relies on human expertise due to the complex nature of seismic data. To alleviate this challenge, there is an increasing need for innovative solutions that collaborate with geoscientists to enhance efficiency. In this study, we introduce a joint inversion-segmentation approach that works in tandem with human experts to segment geologically significant features in seismic data. By employing a cooperative strategy, our method utilizes expert-provided initial guidance in the form of pseudo-labels to refine the segmentation process. We then utilize these segmented features to improve the accuracy of seismic data inversion, which in turn enhances the quality of the segmentation. Through a series of experiments on a 3D real-world dataset, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which achieves a remarkable mean intersection over union score of 0.78 and significantly improves seismic data resolution by a maximum factor of 4.4. Our results indicate that this method effectively captures the continuity of geological structures and produces coherent segmentation maps. Moreover, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of efficiency, requiring 60% less training time and 67% fewer seismic data shots. Our findings suggest that this method offers a promising solution for collaborative seismic data analysis, which can be applied to a wide range of real-world scenarios.
